title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer \(r\ge 1\), does there exist a finite integer \(B(T,r)\) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most \(B(T,r)\)?
definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number \(\omega (G)\) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number \(\chi (G)\) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the induced graph \(G[S]\) retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map \(\varphi :V(T)\to V(G)\) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if \(\varphi (x)\varphi (y)\) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is \(\forall T \forall r \exists B \forall G\): the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |\(V(G)|\), maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function \(f_{T}:N\to N\) with \(\chi (G)\le f_{T}(\omega (G))\) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for \(f_{T}\), or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs \(G_{k}\) satisfying \(\omega (G_{k})\le r\) and \(\chi (G_{k})\to \infty\). A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |\(V(G)|\), or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.

importance.reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.

progress.text: Kierstead–Penrice establish \(\chi\)-boundedness when the excluded tree has radius at most two.
Scott–Seymour strengthen radius-two results under complete multipartite subgraph exclusions; checked preprint revised 10 January 2023.
Nguyen–Scott–Seymour force path-induced rooted copies of arbitrary trees, while permitting extra edges between branches.
Nguyen–Scott–Seymour prove near-linear independent sets and subpolynomial chromatic bounds for every fixed forest and clique bound; journal publication 25 September 2025.
Davies–Yuditsky’s journal publication proves polynomial \(\chi\)-boundedness under the additional promise of boxicity bounded by a fixed dimension.

status_note: The 2025 near-linear-stable-set paper and April 2026 bounded-boxicity paper explicitly retain the general conjecture. The former yields \(n^{o(1)}\) rather than a size-independent bound; the latter restricts the host class. September 2026 results on tournament analogues concern directed parameters. No resolution of this ordinary undirected statement found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size \(n^{1- o(1)}\), and consequently a chromatic bound \(n^{o(1)}\), where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power \(n^{\varepsilon}\) eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also \(n^{o(1)}\) and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant \(B(T,r)\) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.

sentences: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture considers graphs excluding a fixed tree as an induced subgraph.
It asks whether bounding clique number then also bounds chromatic number, independently of graph size.
The proposed principle says that high coloring complexity with no large clique must eventually force every prescribed induced tree.
This would organize a large collection of hereditary coloring classes through one structural mechanism.

The saved review distinguishes genuinely induced trees from weaker path-induced copies and ordinary coloring from fractional results, while allowing an arbitrary bound rather than demanding polynomial growth.
